exam.subject: Agriculture
exam.title: ESSCE 2019 – Agriculture

parts.title: Part I – Multiple Choice Questions
parts.instructions: Part I contains 80 questions; each carries 1 point. There is only one best answer for each question; blacken the letter of your choice on the answer sheet with a pencil.

parts.title: Part II – Short Answer/Essay Questions
parts.instructions: Part II contains seven short answer/essay questions (20 points). Answer all of them on the separate answer sheet.

source.note: Scanned paper; OCR text checked against the page images (garbled items such as Q15, Q44, Q45, Q60, Q65 and Q72 were read from the images). Part II Q3 uses the pig diagram cropped from page 20.

exam.answer_key_note: No official key exists. All answers were solved independently and checked against the Eritrean MoE Agriculture textbooks Grades 11 and 12 (extracted text with page markers). See confidence and review_flag on each question.

questions.stem: An example of a fixed cost of machinery is
explanation_steps: Fixed costs do not change with the amount of output; they are paid even when the machine is not used (textbook: costs of tractors, buildings, equipment, land taxes).
Insurance is paid every year whether the machine works or not, so it is a fixed cost. Fuel, oil/lubricants and repairs rise with hours of use, so they are variable costs. Answer: D.
tips: Machinery fixed costs are often remembered as 'DIRTI': Depreciation, Interest, Repairs-housing (shelter), Taxes, Insurance. Running costs (fuel, oil, repair, labour) are variable.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a variable cost for a farmer who owns a tractor?
explanation_steps: Fuel use rises with the number of hours the tractor works, so it varies with output.
Answer: D.

textbook_ref.section: 4.1 Farm management – categories of cost (fixed and variable costs)

questions.stem: A method of identification or marking that reduces the value of hides and skins in livestock is
explanation_steps: Branding fixes numbers, letters or designs on the skin with a hot iron or chemicals (textbook).
The burn leaves a permanent scar on the skin, so the hide or skin loses value for leather. Ear tags, ear notches and neck straps do not damage the hide. Answer: D.
tips: If a marking method burns or scars the body skin, it lowers hide value.

similar_questions.stem: Which identification method uses a hot iron or chemicals on the skin?
explanation_steps: Textbook: branding fixes marks on the skin with a hot iron or with chemicals.
Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 1.3 Routine management – methods used to identify livestock

questions.stem: Profit of a business is calculated as
explanation_steps: Textbook: net revenue (profit) = total revenue less total cost (TC = fixed cost + variable cost).
Answer: D.
tips: Profit = TR − TC; TR = price × quantity sold.

similar_questions.stem: A farmer sells produce for 40,000 Nakfa; fixed costs are 10,000 Nakfa and variable costs 18,000 Nakfa. The net revenue is
explanation_steps: Net revenue = 40,000 − 28,000 = 12,000 Nakfa. Answer: A.

textbook_ref.section: 4.1 Farm management – categories of cost; net revenue

questions.stem: All of the following are local breeds of livestock in Eritrea except
explanation_steps: Textbook: the cattle breeds in Eritrea are Barka, Arado and Arebo; Dewhin is found on the Sudan border.
White Leghorn is an exotic (imported) egg-laying chicken breed, not a local breed. Answer: C.
tips: Local cattle: Barka, Arado, Arebo, (Dewhin). Local goats: Hassani, Barka (Sudanese desert), Worre, Afar.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is an exotic dairy cattle breed introduced to Eritrea?
explanation_steps: Textbook: the Holstein-Friesian breed has been introduced and is now adapted.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a branch of Plant Science?
explanation_steps: Textbook Table 1.4: plant sciences = horticulture, agronomy, soil science, forestry, forage and pasture; aquaculture (fish farming in ponds) is listed under ANIMAL sciences.
Aquaculture deals with fish and other aquatic animals, so it is clearly not a plant science. Answer: A.
tips: Animal sciences: animal husbandry, nutrition, breeding, aquaculture, rangeland management.

similar_questions.stem: Fish farming in ponds under controlled feeding is called
explanation_steps: Textbook: aquaculture is fish farming in ponds under controlled conditions.
Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: Textbook Table 1.4 places plant protection among the production-support branches, not under plant sciences, so C could also be argued. Aquaculture (animal science) is the clear intended answer.

questions.stem: The science that deals with recording, analyzing and predicting weather over a long period of time, is
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Agro-climatology is the science that deals with recording, analysing and prediction of weather and climatic conditions of an area with the aim of providing information to boost production.'
The other options are processes or land-management practices, not sciences. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Recovering land from the sea or improving degraded land for agriculture is called
explanation_steps: Textbook: land reclamation is a land-management practice used to reclaim/restore land.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following livestock belongs to equines?
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Equines comprise horses, mules and donkeys.' Camels are camelids.
Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Equines are kept in Eritrea mainly for
explanation_steps: Textbook: equines are important for draught and transportation purposes.
Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 1.1.1 Definitions of Livestock and Farm Animals

questions.stem: The highest percentage of area coverage of the different vegetation types in Eritrea is
explanation_steps: Textbook Table 2.3 (vegetation types of Eritrea): bushland 42.7 %, wooded grassland 20.3 %, barren land about 14 %, open woodland 7.6 %, riverine forest 1.5 %.
Bushland covers the largest share. Answer: E.
tips: Order to remember: bushland (≈43 %) > wooded grassland (≈20 %) > barren land > open woodland > forests (< 2 %).

similar_questions.stem: According to the textbook, wooded grassland covers about what share of Eritrea?
explanation_steps: Table 2.3: wooded grassland 25,577 km² ≈ 20.3 %.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following areas still consist of closed to open forest cover in Eritrea?
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Closed to open forest cover still exists in the Semenawi-Bahri and riverine areas.'
Answer: B.
tips: Semenawi Bahri (Green Belt, eastern escarpment) is also a protected area for remnant forests and habitats.

similar_questions.stem: Semenawi Bahri is a protected area mainly for
explanation_steps: Textbook list of protected areas: Semenawi-Bahri – remnant forests and habitats.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: The practice of raising animals to obtain animal products like meat, milk, etc., is
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Animal production, or animal husbandry, is the practice of raising animals to obtain products such as meat, milk, eggs, honey and fish.'
Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: The branch of animal science that improves animals through selection and mating is
explanation_steps: Animal breeding improves production through genetics (selection, crossbreeding).
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 1.1.1 Definitions of Livestock and Farm Animals

questions.stem: Which of the following is a protected area for elephants in Eritrea?
explanation_steps: Textbook protected areas: Gash-Setit (elephants); Semenawi-Bahri (remnant forests); Buri Peninsula (wild ass); Yob and Nakfa (Nubian ibex).
Answer: D.
tips: Match: Gash-Setit – elephant; Buri – wild ass; Yob/Nakfa – Nubian ibex.

similar_questions.stem: The Buri Peninsula is a protected area for the
explanation_steps: Textbook: Buri Peninsula (wild ass).
Answer: B.

questions.stem: A science that examines the origin, classification and description of soil is
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Pedology examines the soil's origin, classification and description'; edaphology studies soil as a medium for plant growth.
Answer: A.
tips: Pedology = soil as a natural body; edaphology = soil for plants.

similar_questions.stem: The study of soil from the point of view of plant growth is
explanation_steps: Edaphology studies the soil as a medium for plant growth.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 2.2.1 Soil Formation – approaches to the study of soil

questions.stem: Which of the following methods optimizes cereal crop seedlings by reducing overpopulation at an early stage of crop growth?
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Thinning involves the removal of some plants so that the remaining plants are able to get enough space and nutrients for good growth' – it reduces competition among crowded seedlings.
Drainage removes water, manuring adds nutrients, budding is a propagation method, rotation changes crops over seasons. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Removing extra seedlings when a crop has emerged too densely is called
explanation_steps: Thinning = removing some plants to reduce competition for light, water and nutrients.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: One of the following is a sedimentary rock.
explanation_steps: Textbook: sedimentary rocks form from deposition and re-cementation of weathered products; sandstone comes from re-cemented quartz sand (also shale, limestone, dolomite).
Granite and basalt are igneous; marble and slate are metamorphic. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Which rock is igneous?
explanation_steps: Textbook: igneous rocks form from molten magma, e.g. granite and basalt.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: A technician took an assignment to determine the germination percentage of maize. He placed a total of 50 seeds in a petri dish out of which 35 seeds germinated. What is the germination percentage of the seed?
explanation_steps: Germination % = (number of seeds germinated ÷ number of seeds tested) × 100.
tips: Do not confuse the number germinated (35) with the percentage.

similar_questions.stem: In a germination test, 84 out of 120 wheat seeds germinated. The germination percentage is
explanation_steps: Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following crops belongs to pulses?
explanation_steps: Pulses are grain legumes (peas, beans, lentils, chickpea).
Sorghum is a cereal, kenaf a fibre crop and elephant grass a forage crop. Answer: E.
tips: Note that the paper repeats 'Sorghum' in A and C.

similar_questions.stem: Which crop is a pulse?
explanation_steps: Lentil is a grain legume (pulse).
Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: Printing error: options A and C are both 'Sorghum'. It does not affect the answer (E).

questions.stem: Which of the following is not the effect of chemical soil degradation?

options.A: Decline in beneficial soil macro and micro flora
options.B: Loss of nutrients and organic matter
options.D: Fixing soluble nutrients making it unavailable to the plant
options.E: Increase on toxic compounds in the soil

explanation_steps: Textbook chemical soil degradation: loss of nutrients and organic matter; fixing of soluble nutrients so they are unavailable to plants; salinization; (toxicity/acidification).
A decline in soil organisms (flora and fauna) is BIOLOGICAL soil degradation. Answer: A.
tips: Physical = compaction, crusting, erosion; chemical = nutrient loss, salinity, toxicity; biological = loss of organic matter and soil organisms.

similar_questions.stem: Salinization of irrigated land is an example of
explanation_steps: Textbook lists salinization under chemical soil degradation.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: The detachment and airborne movement of small soil particles caused by the impact of raindrops on soil is
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Splash erosion is the detachment and airborne movement of small soil particles caused by the impact of raindrops on soil.'
Answer: E.
tips: Sheet erosion adds removal by a thin sheet of runoff; rills are small channels; gullies are deep channels.

similar_questions.stem: Removal of a thin, fairly uniform layer of soil by overland flow is
explanation_steps: Sheet erosion removes soil in thin layers by broad sheets of runoff.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: All of the following are important elements of climate except
explanation_steps: Textbook elements of climate: rainfall, temperature, relative humidity, solar radiation, wind, evaporation, day length.
Photosynthesis is a plant process, not an element of climate. Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is an element of climate?
explanation_steps: Solar radiation is a climatic element; the others are plant processes.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following does not apply to surface irrigation? It is/has

options.B: lower water-use efficiency related to modern irrigation methods.

explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Surface irrigation is usually relatively cheaper to install but more expensive to operate. It has lower water-use efficiency than other methods.'
So A, B and D apply; HIGHER water-use efficiency belongs to modern systems (sprinkler, drip). Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: Compared with surface irrigation, drip irrigation
explanation_steps: Textbook: modern systems are expensive to install but have lower operating costs and higher water-use efficiency.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Kenaf is categorized as a/an
explanation_steps: Textbook: fibre crops are grown for fibres used in textile industries, e.g. cotton, flax, sisal, kenaf.
Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a fibre crop?
explanation_steps: Sisal gives fibre (ropes, sacks).
Answer: A.

questions.stem: One of the following is a type of feed with high fiber content.
explanation_steps: Textbook: feeds with more than 18 % fibre are roughages (bulky); feeds with less than 18 % fibre are concentrates.
Answer: A.
tips: 18 % crude fibre is the dividing line.

similar_questions.stem: Oil-seed cakes and cereal grains are classified as
explanation_steps: Textbook: examples of concentrates include cereal grains, oil-seed cakes and flour-mill by-products.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 1.2.2 Common Classifications and Types of Feeds

questions.stem: Which of the following classifications of forests are not based on biotic interferences?
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Depending on the level of biotic interferences, forests are divided into primary and secondary forests.' Closed/open forests are based on canopy condition; mixed forests on species composition.
So, as printed, B, C, D (and E) are all NOT based on biotic interference, and only A is based on it. The examiner almost certainly meant 'which is based on biotic interference' – keyed A.
tips: Classify by: age (even/uneven aged), species composition (pure/mixed), regeneration (high/coppice/plantation), biotic interference (primary/secondary), canopy (closed/open).

similar_questions.stem: Based on canopy condition, forests are classified as
explanation_steps: Textbook: depending on canopy conditions, forests are closed (stand density > 20 %) or open.
Answer: C.

questions.review_flag: Defective item: as printed ('not based on biotic interference') four options (B, C, D, E) are correct. Primary forest is the only option that IS based on biotic interference; keyed A assuming the word 'not' is an error. Teacher decision needed.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a control measure against ecto-parasites?

options.A: Dipping and spraying livestock with chemicals
options.C: Digging canals around the cattle shed to prevent access of parasites
options.D: Sanitation and hygiene inside and around shed house
options.E: Controlling rodent population in the animal farm

explanation_steps: Textbook tick control: an acaricide canal around the cattle shed; acaricide on newly introduced animals; cleaning/burning vegetation around sheds; controlling rodents (reservoirs of ticks); periodic dipping, spraying, dusting.
Vaccines are used against infectious (bacterial/viral) diseases; ectoparasites are controlled with acaricides and hygiene, not vaccination. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Rodents are controlled on a livestock farm as part of tick control because they

options.C: spread foot and mouth disease only

explanation_steps: Textbook: rodent population should be controlled as they act as reservoirs for ticks.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: The tangible use of forests is

options.B: preventing loss of soil and conserving water.
options.C: shading and cooling effect of a specific place.
options.D: supplying energy source for a village.
options.E: cleaning and improving the quality of air.

explanation_steps: Textbook: intangible roles cannot be measured in money (soil/water protection, climate, noise, air quality); tangible roles are evident and can be valued in money (wood, fuel, fodder, food, gums).
Fuel wood/charcoal supplied to a village is a tangible (marketable) product. Answer: D.
tips: Tangible = you can sell it (timber, fuel wood, fruits, gums, fodder).

similar_questions.stem: Which is an intangible role of forests?
explanation_steps: Soil protection cannot easily be priced – intangible.
Answer: D.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an advantage of using bare roots in raising seedlings?

options.A: Requires less space in the nursery
options.C: Roots are not exposed to air drying in transporting the seedlings
options.D: It is less expensive and cheaper to grow the seedlings
options.E: Soil borne diseases are likely to spread more slowly

explanation_steps: Textbook advantages of bare-root seedlings: less complicated to grow; lighter to transport; each planter carries more; suited to mechanisation and large nurseries; cheaper to produce than potted seedlings.
A, B, C and E are advantages of containerised (potted) seedlings. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Which is a disadvantage of containerised (potted) seedlings?
explanation_steps: Textbook: potted seedlings are heavy to transport and more expensive.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 2.2.6 Seedling Planting – bare-root and container seedlings

questions.stem: Which of the following practices does not contribute to climate change?

options.A: Making use of fuels such as benzene and kerosene

explanation_steps: Burning fossil fuels, fire wood and charcoal and cutting trees release greenhouse gases (CO₂) or reduce CO₂ uptake.
Wind energy is clean and renewable and emits no greenhouse gas. Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a renewable, clean alternative energy source?
explanation_steps: Textbook alternative energy sources include solar, wind and geothermal.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: One of the following is an internal parasite of livestock.
explanation_steps: Textbook: endoparasites live inside the host (roundworms, tapeworms, flukes, protozoa); ectoparasites live on the surface (flies, fleas, ticks, mites, lice).
Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Which of these is an ectoparasite?
explanation_steps: Lice live on the skin surface.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following budget type is used for small changes in any agricultural activity?
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'When a farmer proposes to introduce minor changes to a farm then partial budget can be used to predict the expected change in profits.'
Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: A budget prepared for a whole new farm plan is a
explanation_steps: A complete budget covers the whole farm business.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: All of the following are alternative sources of energy for resolving the conflict between humans and wild life except
explanation_steps: Textbook 2.4.3: alternative energy sources are explored because forest degradation reduced the wood supply; options are solar, wind, geothermal, electricity, kerosene/LPG.
Wood fuel is the conventional source whose over-use destroys wildlife habitat – it is not an alternative. Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: Why is the use of improved (fuel-saving) stoves encouraged in Eritrea?

options.B: To reduce fuel-wood consumption and deforestation

explanation_steps: Less wood burnt → less pressure on forests and wildlife habitats.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: One of the following livestock diseases is neither bacterial nor viral.
explanation_steps: Anthrax, tuberculosis and brucellosis are bacterial; foot and mouth disease is viral (textbook).
Trematodes (flukes) are parasitic flatworms. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Foot and mouth disease is caused by a
explanation_steps: FMD is a viral disease.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Based on their taxonomic grouping, vertebrate wild animals are classified into
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Based on their taxonomic grouping vertebrate wild animals are divided into four major categories: the mammals, birds, reptiles and amphibians.'
Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Based on habitat, wildlife is classified as
explanation_steps: Textbook: aquatic (freshwater, marine) and terrestrial (forest, desert, savannah, mountain).
Answer: B.

questions.stem: The type of animal feed that are cut and offered as fresh or green are
explanation_steps: Textbook: forages such as alfalfa and elephant grass cut and offered fresh are called succulent feeds; dried, they become dry feeds.
Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: Straw of barley and hay are examples of
explanation_steps: Textbook: dry feeds include straws, stovers and hays.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 1.2.2 Common Classifications and Types of Feeds

questions.stem: Which of the following is not among the major causes of deforestation in Eritrea?
explanation_steps: Textbook causes of deforestation: expansion of agriculture, extraction of wood for construction and energy, overgrazing, unsustainable non-wood extraction, lack of tree tenure, climate change and recurrent droughts, war.
All four listed options are causes, so 'None of the above'. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: A lack of tree tenure causes deforestation because

options.B: nobody owns the trees, so no one protects or plants them

explanation_steps: Textbook: without tree tenure, open access leads to inappropriate use and deforestation.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: The practice of removing animals with undesirable characteristics or traits is
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Culling is the practice of removing animals with undesirable characteristics or traits.'
Answer: D.
tips: Selection keeps the best; culling removes the worst.

similar_questions.stem: Mating animals of two different breeds is
explanation_steps: Crossbreeding introduces 'foreign blood'.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: Calculate the annual depreciation of a water pump if the cost is 300,000.00 Nakfa and salvage value is 50,000.00 Nakfa after a life time of 5 years.
explanation_steps: Textbook Equation 4.11: annual depreciation = (cost price − salvage value) ÷ expected lifetime.
tips: 250,000 (B) is the total depreciation over 5 years; 60,000 (D) forgets the salvage value.

similar_questions.stem: A sprayer costs 80,000 Nakfa, lasts 6 years and has a salvage value of 8,000 Nakfa. The annual straight-line depreciation is
explanation_steps: Answer: B.

questions.stem: All of the following apply to cooperatives except that they are

options.A: autonomous association with members are organized voluntarily.
options.B: meet their common economic, social and cultural objectives.
options.C: organized based upon personal ties and mutual thrust.
options.D: owned and controlled by members for their own benefits.

explanation_steps: Textbook: a co-operative is an autonomous association of persons united voluntarily to meet common economic, social and cultural objectives through jointly owned and democratically controlled enterprises; it is based on close personal ties and mutual trust.
Being autonomous and member-owned, a co-operative is neither a charity nor state-directed. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: 'Everyone who fulfils the requirements may join on a voluntary basis' is the co-operative principle of
explanation_steps: Textbook: voluntary and open membership.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: A branch of Animal Science that deals with a balanced diet of livestock for higher milk/meat yield is
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Animal nutrition concerns the feeding of farm animals a balanced diet in order to achieve optimum production.'
Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Preventing and treating animal diseases is the concern of
explanation_steps: Veterinary science deals with animal health.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following farming types does not exist in Eritrea?
explanation_steps: Textbook: Eritrea's major farming systems are nomadic pastoralism, semi-nomadic pastoralism and sedentary agro-pastoralism, plus intensive systems; farmers are mostly subsistence (about 95 % of cultivated land), with some commercial and arable (crop) farming.
Ranching – large fenced commercial grazing estates – is not practised in Eritrea. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Which farming system involves the largest share (about 67 %) of the Eritrean population?
explanation_steps: Table 1.1: nomadic 11 %, semi-nomadic 22 %, sedentary agro-pastoralism 67 %.
Answer: C.

questions.review_flag: The textbook does not state explicitly that ranching is absent; it simply is not among the farming systems described for Eritrea. Keyed B.

questions.stem: One of the following is a practice when animals suspected to be infected with contagious diseases are separated from healthy ones.
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Isolation – animals that are known or suspected to be infected with a contagious disease must be isolated from the healthy ones.'
Quarantine separates seemingly HEALTHY animals that were exposed to infection (e.g. newly bought animals) to see whether they harbour infection. Answer: C.
tips: Isolation = sick or suspected sick; quarantine = healthy-looking but exposed/newly introduced.

similar_questions.stem: Newly purchased, healthy-looking goats kept apart for some weeks before joining the flock are under
explanation_steps: Separating seemingly healthy, possibly exposed animals is quarantine.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 1.5.2 Prevention and Control Measures – isolation, quarantine

questions.review_flag: Quarantine (B) is often used loosely for this idea; the textbook's own wording ('known or suspected to be infected … isolated') matches C. Keyed C.

questions.stem: Which of the following meteorological equipment measures the pressure in the air?
explanation_steps: A barometer measures atmospheric (air) pressure.
Rain gauge – rainfall; anemometer – wind speed; thermometer – temperature; a seismometer records earthquakes and is not a weather instrument. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Which instrument measures relative humidity?
explanation_steps: A hygrometer (or wet- and dry-bulb thermometer) measures relative humidity.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: If the term "fauna" refers to animal life, the corresponding term for plant life is
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Flora refers to all forms of plant', from microscopic algae and fungi to trees; fauna refers to animal life.
Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: Elephants, leopards and gazelles of an area are part of its
explanation_steps: Animal life = fauna.
Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: Option E is illegible in the scan (read as 'zoo'); it does not affect the answer.

questions.stem: A practice of growing crops without the use of soil as a medium for their growth is
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Hydroponics – a system where crops are grown without use of soil as a medium for plant growth; all essential nutrients are provided in solution form.'
Hydrophytes, mesophytes and xerophytes are plant types by water requirement; 'hydrophobic' means water-repelling. Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: Growing horticultural crops in greenhouses or shade houses is called
explanation_steps: Textbook horticultural production systems: open field, protected areas, hydroponics.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Groundnut can be used for the following sources of food except for
explanation_steps: Groundnut (peanut) is an oil crop (textbook). The seeds are pressed for edible oil, ground into peanut butter, roasted/salted as snacks and confections, and used to flavour sauces and dishes.
Groundnut contains little starch and no gluten, so it is not used to make bread (that is the role of wheat and other cereals). Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Groundnut is classified as a/an
explanation_steps: Textbook: oil crops include cottonseed, sesame, groundnut, Niger seed and linseed.
Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: The textbook only classifies groundnut as an oil crop; its other food uses (butter, confections, flavouring) come from general knowledge. 'Flavor enhancer' (D) is vague, but E is the clear non-use.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a trace element required in small quantities by plants?
explanation_steps: Textbook: micronutrients (trace elements) are manganese, iron, molybdenum, copper, boron, zinc and chlorine.
Magnesium is a macronutrient (secondary nutrient, with calcium and sulphur). Answer: E.
tips: Do not confuse magnesium (Mg, macro) with manganese (Mn, micro).

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a primary macronutrient?
explanation_steps: Primary nutrients: N, P, K.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: One of the following characteristics does not apply to weeds.

options.B: Weeds compete for nutrient and moisture.
options.D: Weeds harbor insect and disease causing micro-organisms.

explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Weeds can be harmful or beneficial. They are harmful because they harbour insects and disease-causing micro-organisms, and compete …'; benefits include feed, medicine, compost, soil cover.
So B, C and D apply; the claim that no weed is beneficial is false. Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: Which is a beneficial use of some weeds?
explanation_steps: Some weeds are used as animal feed, medicine or compost.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following horticultural crops is highly perishable and susceptible to post harvest problems?
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Some crops are highly perishable (tomato, strawberry, guava, etc.), whereas others are not (onion, potato, pumpkin).'
Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Which crop can be packed in sacks for transport because it is not highly perishable?
explanation_steps: Textbook: potatoes and onions can be packed in sacks.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an appropriate land-use planning procedure?

options.A: Use of fertile lands for house construction
options.B: Cultivation of crops on steep slopes
options.C: Designing human settlements and allocation of agricultural land

explanation_steps: Textbook: proper land-use planning ensures the correct allocation of land for different uses (crops, livestock, forest, settlement) considering the ecosystem's carrying capacity.
A, B, D and E are forms of land misuse that cause degradation. Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: The main purpose of land-use planning on a farm is to
explanation_steps: Textbook: land-use planning specifies uses of farmland (crop, vegetable, livestock, woodland).
Answer: B.

questions.stem: The branch of agriculture that deals with the principles and practices of field crop production and crop husbandry is
explanation_steps: Agronomy is the branch of plant science dealing with field crop production and soil management (crop husbandry).
Horticulture deals with fruits, vegetables and ornamentals. Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: Production of fruits, vegetables and flowers is the concern of
explanation_steps: Horticulture = garden crops.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements describes the importance of biodiversity conservation? Biodiversity is a

options.C: foundation for domestication of plants and animals.

explanation_steps: Textbook 2.3.2 importance of biodiversity: food, medicine, raw materials, genetic resources for domestication and breeding, income, and pristine habitats as tourist attractions.
Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Conserving crops in gene banks is called
explanation_steps: Textbook: ex-situ = in gene banks; in-situ = on farmers' fields and enclosures.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: One of the following is not an ecological role of soils?

options.B: Recycling of nutrient and organic matter

explanation_steps: Textbook Figure 2.2 shows the five major ecological roles of soil: medium for plant growth, regulator of water supplies, recycler of nutrients and organic wastes, habitat for soil organisms and engineering medium (supports buildings and roads).
Soil filters pollutants from water, but 'cleaning air pollution' is not one of the five roles. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Supporting roads and buildings is the soil's role as
explanation_steps: Soil acts as an engineering medium.
Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: The five roles are shown only in textbook Figure 2.2 (image, not in the extracted text); the text also mentions that plants in soil fix CO₂. Keyed D.

questions.stem: All of following are preconditions in the selection of a particular variety for crops except that the variety should be

options.A: well adapted to the growing area.
options.D: susceptible to biotic and abiotic factors.

explanation_steps: Textbook seed/variety selection: adapted to the growing area; desirable characters (earliness, quality, yield); free from diseases and pests; RESISTANT to abiotic factors (cold, frost, heat, drought, salinity); market demand.
A variety should be resistant, not susceptible. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: A farmer in a drought-prone lowland should choose a variety that is
explanation_steps: Adapted, early maturing, stress-resistant varieties suit dry areas.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following does not apply to No-till farming practices? It

options.B: maintains soil structure and control erosion

explanation_steps: Textbook advantages of no-till: maintains soil structure and controls erosion; conserves moisture; increases nitrogen availability; minimizes cost of production; reduces CO₂ emission; higher grain yield.
No-till MINIMIZES soil disturbance (seed placed in a narrow slot). Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: No-tillage means

options.B: planting in previously untilled soil through a narrow slot

explanation_steps: Textbook definition of no-tillage.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: If the name "Arado" refers to the local cattle breed, ______ refers to the local goat breed.
explanation_steps: Textbook: goat breeds in Eritrea include the Hassani (Shukria), the Sudanese Desert (Barka/Tsa'adi), Worre and Afar; the Hassani is known for milk and twinning.
Arebo and Dewhin are cattle breeds. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Which Eritrean goat breed is known for milk production and frequent twins and triplets?
explanation_steps: Textbook: the Hassani.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a benefit of organic matter in the soil? It

options.B: facilitates the increase in infiltration rate.
options.D: reduces moisture storage in the soil.

explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Increased organic matter in the soil improves water retention capacity, facilitates an increase in the infiltration rate and reduces runoff.'
Organic matter INCREASES moisture storage. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Adding compost to a sandy soil mainly
explanation_steps: Humus holds water and nutrients.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 3.1.2 The Importance of Soil and Water Conservation

questions.stem: All of the following are consequences of soil erosion except that it

options.B: reduces the soil moisture storage capacity and infiltration rate.
options.C: affects the anchorage of crops in the soil.

explanation_steps: Textbook consequences of soil erosion: loss of fertile topsoil and organic matter, reduced moisture storage and infiltration, shallower soils (poor anchorage), lower yields.
Erosion degrades, not improves, vegetation cover. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Which practice reduces soil erosion on hillsides?
explanation_steps: Terraces reduce slope length and runoff speed.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: The removal of water from waterlogged areas by using water demanding vegetation is
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Bio-drainage … the removal of water from waterlogged areas by using vegetation such as trees with high water requirements (e.g. Eucalyptus spp.).'
Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Removing excess water from the land surface with shallow open ditches is
explanation_steps: Textbook: surface drainage uses shallow ditches (open drains).
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a physical soil and water conservation measure?
explanation_steps: Textbook Table 3.2 lists physical conservation measures: terraces, stone bunds, diversion ditches, waterways, gully control, live fencing.
Crop rotation is an agronomic (biological) practice. Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: Which is a biological (vegetative) SWC measure?
explanation_steps: Textbook vegetative measures: enclosures, afforestation, agronomic measures, agroforestry.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: A system of irrigation practiced in the lowlands involving the diversion of flowing water into crop fields when it rains in the highlands is
explanation_steps: Spate irrigation diverts seasonal flood (spate) flows – generated by highland rain – from ephemeral rivers into lowland fields, e.g. Sheeb (Northern Red Sea) and Gash-Barka.
Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Sheeb in the Northern Red Sea zone is known for
explanation_steps: Textbook: semi-nomadic pastoralism occurs in spate irrigation areas such as Sheeb.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which one of the following soil types could be subjected to water logging?
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Soils that are predominantly clay filter water very slowly downward, meanwhile plant roots suffocate' – clay soils waterlog.
Sand and sandy loam drain freely. Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: Which soil has the highest drainage (infiltration) rate?
explanation_steps: Large pores in sand drain water fast.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: A water body created by excavating a pit or by constructing a short embankment across a water source is a
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Ponds are bodies of water created by excavating a pit or by constructing a short embankment across a water source.' In Eritrea they hold 500–5000 m³.
Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: A structure built across a river to divert regulated quantities of water towards a canal is a
explanation_steps: Textbook 3.4.3 river diversion.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: The full exploitation of livestock resources in Eritrea has been challenged due to

options.B: the presence of wide spread chronic livestock diseases.
options.C: the breeds of livestock that can survive under shortage of input.
options.D: housing of livestock which does not limit the output of livestock.
options.E: inadequate health care services that limit production of livestock.

explanation_steps: Textbook constraints on livestock: 'a shortage of feed (both in quality and quantity), the presence of widespread diseases and unimproved animal breeds. Most livestock also receive little inputs in terms of feeding, healthcare and housing, which limits the output.'

C and D are false (they describe non-constraints). But A (poor feed quality), B (widespread diseases) and E (inadequate health care) all match the textbook. B follows the wording 'presence of widespread diseases' most closely – keyed B, with A and E also accepted.
tips: Constraints: feed shortage, widespread diseases, unimproved breeds, low inputs (feed, health care, housing).

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a constraint on livestock production in Eritrea according to the textbook?

options.E: High per-capita consumption of animal products

explanation_steps: Eritrea is among the lowest consumers of animal products per capita.
Answer: E.

textbook_ref.section: 1.1.2 Livestock Status and Population in Eritrea

questions.review_flag: Defective item: A (poor feed quality), B (widespread diseases) and E (inadequate health care) are all constraints named in the textbook and there is no 'all of the above'. Keyed B; A and E also accepted. Teacher decision needed.

questions.stem: Which of the following is correct about vaccines in animal health?

options.A: They are meant mainly to treat viral and bacterial diseases.
options.C: An animal has to be sick to be vaccinated.
options.D: The vaccines treat the animals against several diseases.

explanation_steps: Textbook: immunization renders animals resistant to diseases using vaccines and antisera; immunity is the power to resist infection.
A vaccine stimulates the immune system of a HEALTHY animal to prevent disease; it does not treat disease, and each vaccine targets a specific disease. Answer: B.
tips: Vaccines prevent; drugs treat.

similar_questions.stem: Vaccination is most useful when given

options.B: to healthy animals before exposure to the disease

explanation_steps: Vaccines build immunity in advance.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: In the interaction between trees and wild animals, Amensalism refers to the association where

options.A: competition exists among species for water, food and nutrients.
options.B: plants provide a nesting opportunity or shelter to animals.
options.C: neither trees nor wild animals are negatively affected.
options.D: the first species is neither affected nor benefited while the second one is affected negatively.
options.E: parasites and predators affect each other.

explanation_steps: Textbook Table 2.1: amensalism (0, −) – the first species is neither affected nor benefiting while the second is affected negatively.
Answer: D.
tips: Mutualism +/+; commensalism +/0; amensalism 0/−; competition −/−; parasitism/predation +/−; neutralism 0/0.

similar_questions.stem: An interaction in which one species benefits and the other is unaffected is
explanation_steps: Commensalism (+, 0).
Answer: B.

questions.stem: All of the following are the pillars of food security except

options.A: sufficient amount of food produced and prices are not affordable.
options.B: sufficient quantities of food is produced.
options.C: nutritious types of food are produced.
options.D: food is available at affordable prices.
options.E: sufficient amount of food is produced and prices are affordable.

explanation_steps: Food security requires enough food (availability), good nutritional quality (utilisation) and access – food that people can afford.
If prices are NOT affordable, people lack access, so A contradicts food security. Answer: A.
tips: Pillars: availability, access (affordability), utilisation (nutrition), stability.

similar_questions.stem: A country produces enough grain but most households cannot afford to buy it. Which pillar of food security is missing?
explanation_steps: Affordability = economic access.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 1.2 Role of Agriculture in Eritrea – food supply and food security
textbook_ref.note: The textbook raises food security in activities but does not list its pillars; answer based on the standard definition.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is true about highland forests? They are

options.A: composed of acacia and associated tree species.
options.B: vegetation types dominated by short and thorny acacias.
options.C: part of montane forests composed of tree species mixed with Juniperus procera and Olea africana.
options.D: sparsely populated woody vegetation with open grassland.
options.E: forests found in major river banks and seasonal floods.

explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Highland forests are mainly dry montane forest composed of a mixture of coniferous tree species such as Juniperus procera and broad-leaved species such as Olea africana.'
A = mixed woodlands; B = bush/shrub vegetation; D = wooded grassland; E = riverine forests. Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: Mixed woodlands of acacia and associated species occur mainly in the
explanation_steps: Textbook: mixed woodlands occur in the western and south-western lowlands.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not practiced under permanent area closures?

options.A: Buffer area is created at the periphery of the closure.
options.B: Local communities are allowed to cut and carry animal feed.
options.C: Controlled grazing is practiced with periodic resting of closures.
options.D: Plant species difficult for grazing are selectively removed.
options.E: Permanent area closures are divided into various blocks.

explanation_steps: Textbook management of a permanent closure (forest): demarcate boundaries; create a buffer area at the periphery; plant valuable species in gaps; allow communities to cut and carry grass; remove unwanted plant species; divide into blocks/fire-line compartments.
Rotational (controlled) grazing with periodic resting is a rangeland/temporary-closure practice; permanent closures exclude livestock (cut-and-carry instead). Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: In a permanent closure, villagers usually obtain grass by
explanation_steps: Textbook: local communities should be allowed to cut and carry grasses.
Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: The textbook list ends with 'unwanted plant species should be removed … and optional grazing tried', so C is not absolutely excluded; it is the option least consistent with permanent closures. Keyed C.

questions.stem: In Agriculture, if the slope of an area is 20 percent it can be categorized as
explanation_steps: Textbook slope classes: 0–8 % level to gently undulating; 8–30 % rolling to hilly; > 30 % steeply dissected to mountainous.
20 % lies between 8 and 30 %. Answer: D.
tips: Slope % = vertical interval ÷ horizontal distance × 100.

similar_questions.stem: A field rises 9 m over a horizontal distance of 50 m. Its slope and class are
explanation_steps: 18 % is in the 8–30 % class: rolling to hilly. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not an advantage of intensive or conventional housing of livestock?

options.A: Animals are secured at neck to neck direction with chains/ ropes.
options.B: Animals are kept lose in an open paddock except during milking.
options.C: The cows are fed and milked in the animal barn.
options.D: The animals are arranged in both a single row and double row.
options.E: The structure is built so that it becomes suitable for milking.

explanation_steps: Textbook intensive (conventional) housing: cows confined on a platform and secured at the neck with chains or ropes; fed and milked in the barn; structure suitable for milking; single row (< 10 cows) or double row.
Keeping animals loose in an open paddock except during milking is the LOOSE housing system. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Which is an advantage of loose housing over conventional housing?
explanation_steps: Textbook: loose housing is cheaper, easy to expand and facilitates heat detection.
Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: The options describe features of the system rather than 'advantages'; the only option not belonging to intensive housing is B.

questions.stem:
Questions 70 and 71 refer to the table: fertilizer levels (kg/ha) applied to sorghum and the total product obtained (kg/ha). Fertilizer level (kg/ha) → total product of sorghum (kg/ha): 2 → 20; 4 → 32; 6 → 36; 8 → 34.
Calculate the Marginal Product (MP) at 4 kg/ha fertilizer level?
explanation_steps: MP = change in total product ÷ change in input (textbook Equation 4.5).
From 2 to 4 kg/ha: ΔTP = 32 − 20 = 12 kg/ha for ΔX = 2 kg/ha of fertilizer.
Strictly, MP = 12 ÷ 2 = 6 kg of sorghum per kg of fertilizer – not among the options.
The examiner took the added product for the step (ΔTP = 12 kg/ha), as when inputs rise by one 'unit' of 2 kg. Answer: D.
tips: If the input steps are not 1 unit, divide ΔTP by ΔX; in this paper the options only fit ΔTP per step.

similar_questions.stem: From textbook Table 4.2, fertilizer rises from 2 to 3 kg/ha and maize TP from 20 to 28 kg/ha. The MP is
explanation_steps: Answer: C.

questions.review_flag: With the textbook formula MP = ΔTP/ΔX the answer is 6 kg per kg of fertilizer, which is not offered; D (12 = ΔTP per 2-kg step) is the intended key. Units in the options are loose.

questions.stem:
Questions 70 and 71 refer to the table: fertilizer levels (kg/ha) applied to sorghum and the total product obtained (kg/ha). Fertilizer level (kg/ha) → total product of sorghum (kg/ha): 2 → 20; 4 → 32; 6 → 36; 8 → 34.
Calculate the Marginal Value Product (MVP) at a fertilizer level of 6 kg/ha if the price is 5.00 Nakfa per kg.
explanation_steps: MVP = MP × price of output (textbook Equation 4.6).
From 4 to 6 kg/ha: ΔTP = 36 − 32 = 4 kg/ha.
Using the paper's convention (ΔTP per step, as in Q70): MVP = 4 × 5 = 20 Nakfa. Strictly, MP = 4 ÷ 2 = 2 kg per kg → MVP = 10 Nakfa, which is not offered.
Answer: A (the unit should be Nakfa, not kg/ha).
tips: MVP is money (Nakfa), not kg/ha. Negative MVP (−10) would occur at 8 kg/ha, where TP falls from 36 to 34.

similar_questions.stem: From textbook Table 4.2, fertilizer rises from 4 to 5 kg/ha and maize TP from 32 to 35 kg/ha; maize sells at 5 Nakfa/kg. The MVP is
explanation_steps: MVP = 3 × 5 = 15 Nakfa. Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 4.1 Optimum input usage – marginal value product (Equation 4.6)

questions.review_flag: Strict MVP = (4 ÷ 2) × 5 = 10 Nakfa is not offered; A (20) follows the ΔTP-per-step convention used for Q70. The options wrongly carry the unit kg/ha instead of Nakfa.

questions.stem: One of the following is not a fixed resource in the process of agricultural commodity production.
explanation_steps: Textbook: fixed costs/resources (tractors, buildings, equipment, machinery, land) do not change with the level of output; variable inputs (fertilizers, insecticides, fuel) change with production.
Fertiliser is a variable resource. Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a variable input?
explanation_steps: Seed quantity changes with the area and level of production.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following methods of farming has a long thin piece of land across the contours planted with different types of crops in order to reduce soil erosion?
explanation_steps: Strip cropping grows alternating long, narrow strips of different crops (e.g. a cereal and a close-growing legume or grass) across the slope along the contours; the dense strips slow runoff and trap soil.
Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Covering the soil surface with crop residues or straw to reduce evaporation and erosion is
explanation_steps: Mulching (textbook Figure 3.13).
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.note: The textbook lists agronomic conservation measures (vegetative cover, mulching) but does not describe strip cropping by name.

questions.stem: All of the following are dicotyledonous crops except
explanation_steps: Textbook: most cereals such as barley, maize and wheat are monocots; dicots (two cotyledons) include beans and peas.
Chickpea, peanut, broad bean and lentil are legumes (dicots). Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Which crop is a monocot?
explanation_steps: Sorghum is a cereal (grass) – monocot.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: The type of fertilizer that uses solid and liquid excreta of livestock mixed with litter is
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Farmyard manure is a solid and liquid excreta of livestock mixed with litter.'
Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Partially decomposed plant, animal or human material used as organic fertilizer is
explanation_steps: Textbook definition of compost.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: According to 'Vavilov', the Russian scientist, Eritrea is a center of diversity for
explanation_steps: Textbook: Vavilov confirmed the Abyssinian plateau, including Eritrea, as a centre of diversity for barley, emmer and other tetraploid wheats, oats, linseed, safflower, chickpea, lentil, grass pea, pea, horse bean, rapeseed and mustard.
Maize and potato come from the Americas; banana from Asia. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Which crops originated on the Abyssinian plateau including Eritrea?
explanation_steps: Textbook: sorghum, okra, taff, Niger seed and sesame originated in the Abyssinian plateau.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: The smallest river basin in terms of catchment area in Eritrea is
explanation_steps: Textbook Table 2.12: Setit 4,045 km²; Danakil 10,530 km²; Mereb-Gash 23,200 km² (16,730 in Eritrea); Barka-Anseba 39,510 km²; Red Sea 44,690 km².
Setit is the smallest (and the only perennial). Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: The largest river basin of Eritrea by area is the
explanation_steps: Table 2.12: Red Sea basin 44,690 km².
Answer: D.

textbook_ref.section: 2.4.3 The Major River Basins of Eritrea (Table 2.12)

questions.stem: All of the following are direct soil forming factors except
explanation_steps: Textbook: soil is formed as a function of parent material, climate, biota (organisms) and topography acting over time.
The greenhouse effect is not a soil-forming factor. Answer: D.
tips: Remember 'ClORPT': Climate, Organisms, Relief (topography), Parent material, Time.

similar_questions.stem: Which of these is one of the five soil-forming factors?
explanation_steps: Parent material, climate, organisms, topography and time.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following instruments quickly measures the percentage of slope by taking the vertical interval and gradients?
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Clinometer – a hand-held instrument used to quickly measure percentage slope. It can also give an approximate measure of vertical interval and gradients.'
Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Which SWC surveying instrument uses a water-filled transparent tube?
explanation_steps: The flexible-tube (water) level.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following themes applies to biodiversity in Eritrea?

options.A: Proper identification and classification of biodiversity.
options.B: Management of pollution in relation to biodiversity.
options.C: Create public awareness and provide education on biodiversity.

explanation_steps: Textbook: Eritrea's biodiversity strategy has 10 themes, including taxonomic knowledge (proper identification and classification), pollution management, public awareness and education, and sustainable use of natural resources.
Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Conserving crops and trees on farmers' fields or in protected areas is the biodiversity theme of
explanation_steps: Textbook: in-situ conservation.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 2.3.1 Terrestrial Biodiversity – biodiversity themes in Eritrea

questions.stem: List down the classification groups of plants based on their day length and photoperiodic responses. (1.5 points)
questions.answer:
1. Short-day plants – develop (flower, form tubers etc.) with less than 12 hours of daylight.
2. Long-day plants – develop and produce normally when the photoperiod is greater than 12 hours of light.
3. Day-neutral plants – unaffected by photoperiod; they grow and flower over a wide range of day lengths.

subparts.question: Group 3
subparts.answer: Day-neutral plants (not affected by day length).
steps: Flower over a wide range of day lengths.

explanation_steps: Textbook 'Classification based on day length': short-day, long-day and day-neutral plants.
0.5 point for each group (a short definition makes the answer complete).
marking_points: 0.5 each: short-day plants; long-day plants; day-neutral plants.
tips: Some crops (e.g. onion) have both short-day (tropical) and long-day (high-latitude) varieties.

similar_questions.stem: Why do long-day plants often fail to flower when grown in the tropics?
similar_questions.answer: Tropical day length stays close to 12 hours, never long enough to trigger flowering, so the plants remain vegetative.
explanation_steps: Textbook: it is useless to attempt to grow long-day plants in the tropics; they remain vegetative.

textbook_ref.section: 3.1 Environmental factors – classification based on day length

questions.stem:
Write three main reasons for making identifications such as tagging and tattooing in livestock? (3 points)
2.1 ______
2.2 ______
2.3 ______
questions.answer:
2.1 To identify each animal individually (know which animal is which, and its owner – helps prevent theft and settle ownership).
2.2 For certification of animals (e.g. registration of pedigree/breed, sale, vaccination and health certificates).
2.3 To keep accurate records of each animal (breeding, production, feeding, health and treatment records) for management decisions such as selection and culling.

subparts.question: Reason 3
subparts.answer: Keeping accurate records of each animal.

explanation_steps: Textbook: 'The purpose of identification is: identification of animals; certification of animals; keeping records of each animal accurately.'
Common methods: tattooing, tagging, ear-notching and branding.
1 point for each reason.
marking_points: 1 point each: identification of individual animals/ownership; certification (registration, sale, health certificates); accurate record keeping (production, breeding, health) for selection and management.
tips: Records need identities: you cannot record milk yield or calving of 'the brown cow' in a large herd.

similar_questions.stem: Name the livestock identification method best suited to cattle, camels and horses that uses a hot iron, and give one disadvantage.
similar_questions.answer: Branding; it damages the hide/skin and lowers its value (and causes pain).
explanation_steps: Textbook: branding is most suited to cattle, buffalo, horses and camels.

textbook_ref.section: 1.3 Routine management – methods used to identify livestock

questions.stem:
Label the digestive system of a pig. (3 points)
[Diagram: outline of a pig with three labelled parts: 3.1 – the tube running from the mouth along the neck; 3.2 – the large sac-shaped organ in the middle of the body; 3.3 – the first coiled section leading from that sac, in front of the larger coils near the tail.]
questions.image_alt: Outline drawing of a pig showing its digestive tract: label 3.1 points to the oesophagus running from the mouth along the neck; label 3.2 points to the sac-shaped stomach in the middle of the body; label 3.3 points to the first coiled loops leaving the stomach (small intestine), in front of the large coiled mass near the tail (large intestine).

subparts.question: Label 3.2
steps: Single stomach of a monogastric animal.

explanation_steps: The pig's digestive tract has five main parts: mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small and large intestines (textbook Figure 1.2).
3.1 is the tube from the mouth to the stomach = oesophagus.
3.2 is the single, sac-like stomach (pigs are monogastric).
3.3 points to the coils leaving the stomach = small intestine (the larger coils further back are the large intestine).
1 point per correct label.
marking_points: 1 point each: 3.1 oesophagus; 3.2 stomach; 3.3 small intestine.
tips: The diagram matches textbook Figure 1.2 (mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine).

similar_questions.stem: Why is the pig described as monogastric, and what kind of feed does it need?
similar_questions.answer: It has one simple stomach (mono = one, gastric = stomach), like humans; it cannot digest much fibre, so it needs grains and other feeds with little or no fibre.
explanation_steps: Textbook: pigs cannot live on grasses and pasture as ruminants do.

textbook_ref.section: 1.1.4 Types and Classification of Livestock – digestive system of pigs (Figure 1.2)

questions.stem:
Name and define the two methods of plant genetic conservation measures. (2 points)
4.1 ______
4.2 ______
questions.answer:
4.1 Ex-situ conservation – conserving genetic resources (seeds, plant material) outside their natural habitat, e.g. in gene banks.
4.2 In-situ conservation – conserving genetic resources in their natural habitat, i.e. on farmers' fields and in enclosures/protected areas.

subparts.question: Method 1
subparts.answer: Ex-situ: conservation in gene banks (outside the natural habitat).

subparts.question: Method 2
subparts.answer: In-situ: conservation on farmers' fields and in enclosures (natural habitat).

explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Two methods used to offset this genetic loss: ex-situ and in-situ conservation measures. Ex-situ means conserving genetic resource in gene banks. In-situ refers to conserving genetic resources on farmers' fields and in enclosure areas.'
0.5 for each name + 0.5 for each definition.
marking_points: 4.1 (1): ex-situ named (0.5) + conservation outside natural habitat / in gene banks (0.5).
4.2 (1): in-situ named (0.5) + conservation on farmers' fields / enclosures / natural habitat (0.5).
tips: Ex = outside (gene bank); in = inside the natural place (field, enclosure).

similar_questions.stem: Give one advantage of in-situ conservation over ex-situ conservation.
similar_questions.answer: The crops/plants keep evolving and adapting to local conditions (and farmers keep using them); it is cheaper than storing seed in a gene bank.
explanation_steps: In-situ keeps the natural evolutionary process going.

questions.stem:
Give an example of one crop each that can be used as raw material for the following industries. (4 points)
5.1 Textile industry
5.2 Pasta industry
5.3 Brewing industry
5.4 Edible oil industry
questions.answer:
5.1 Textile industry: cotton (also flax, kenaf, sisal).
5.2 Pasta industry: wheat (durum wheat).
5.3 Brewing industry: barley (malting barley); sorghum is also used.
5.4 Edible oil industry: sesame (also cottonseed, Niger seed, groundnut, linseed, sunflower).
explanation_steps: Textbook: agriculture is the basis of textile, brewery and food-processing industries; 'Edible oil is extracted from sesame, cottonseed and Niger seed. Wheat and other grains are used in the manufacturing of flour and pasta. Malting barley is used for the manufacture of beer.'
Fibre crops (cotton, flax, sisal, kenaf) supply the textile industry.
1 point for each correct crop.
marking_points: 1 each: 5.1 cotton/flax/kenaf/sisal; 5.2 wheat (durum); 5.3 barley (malting) or sorghum; 5.4 sesame/cottonseed/Niger seed/groundnut/linseed/sunflower.

similar_questions.stem: Name the crop used as raw material by the sugar industry.
explanation_steps: Sugar is processed from sugarcane.

questions.stem: Explain how population pressure can be considered as the main cause of land degradation. (2.5 points)
questions.answer: A growing population needs more food, fuel, housing and grazing. To meet this demand, (1) cultivation expands onto marginal land and steep slopes that were previously unsuitable, and fallow periods are shortened (continuous cropping); (2) more trees are cut for fire wood, charcoal and construction (deforestation); (3) more livestock are kept, so grazing exceeds carrying capacity (overgrazing); (4) land holdings become small and fragmented and farmers cannot afford conservation. These activities remove vegetation cover, expose the soil to erosion and exhaust nutrients and organic matter, so the land degrades. (The textbook notes that it is what people do to the land – not numbers alone – that determines degradation; well-motivated people can also reverse it.)
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'One view considers population pressure to be the main cause of deforestation, overgrazing and expansion of cultivation into marginal lands.'
G12 p105: increasing population pressure extended land clearing to steep areas; a growing population raises demand for fire wood and timber.
Link each pressure to the degradation it causes: clearing slopes → erosion; wood demand → deforestation; more livestock → overgrazing; continuous cropping → nutrient depletion.
About 0.5 point per well-explained link (five links) or equivalent.
marking_points: 0.5 each (max 2.5): expansion of cultivation onto marginal/steep land; deforestation for fuel wood and construction; overgrazing (livestock beyond carrying capacity); continuous cropping/shortened fallow and nutrient depletion; land fragmentation/poverty limiting conservation; resulting loss of vegetation cover and erosion.
tips: Chain: more people → more demand → misuse of land → loss of cover → erosion/nutrient loss → degraded land.

similar_questions.stem: Give two ways in which people can help reverse land degradation.
similar_questions.answer: Any two: building terraces and stone bunds; afforestation and area closures; controlled grazing; using improved stoves/alternative energy; applying manure and crop rotation.
explanation_steps: Textbook: people can be a major asset in reversing degradation if motivated.

questions.stem: Explain briefly the classification of wild life based on their habitat? (4 points)
questions.answer:
Based on habitat, wildlife is classified into two groups:
1. Aquatic wildlife – animals and plants that live in water: (a) freshwater wildlife (rivers, lakes, ponds, dams, e.g. fish, crocodiles, water birds) and (b) marine wildlife (sea, e.g. dugong, dolphins, sea turtles, corals, fish of the Red Sea).
2. Terrestrial wildlife – wildlife living on land: (a) forest wildlife (e.g. leopards, monkeys, bushbuck), (b) desert wildlife (e.g. dorcas gazelle, ostrich, wild ass), (c) savannah wildlife (e.g. elephants, gazelles, kudu) and (d) mountain wildlife (e.g. Nubian ibex, klipspringer).
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Based on their habitat, wildlife can be classified as: aquatic (freshwater and marine wildlife); terrestrial wildlife (forest, desert, savannah and mountain wildlife).'
Explain each main group (1 point each) and its sub-groups with examples (about 2 points in total).
marking_points: 1: freshwater and marine sub-groups with examples.
1: forest, desert, savannah and mountain sub-groups with examples.
tips: Two main groups, six sub-groups: freshwater, marine | forest, desert, savannah, mountain.
